summary: Describes requirements for multi-segment pseudowires, which extend the reach of pseudowires across multiple domains. The domains can be autonomous systems under one or several providers, IGP areas, or administratively set up pseudowire domains. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A pseudowire is a virtual wire drawn across a packet network. Usually it runs in one piece from one end to the other. This memo covers the harder case where it has to be stitched together from several pieces, each in a different network, and says what the pieces have to support.

subtitle: What a pseudowire solution must do to stretch one virtual wire across several networks, joined end to end.

tldr.problem: A pseudowire normally runs across one packet network between two provider edges. Real deployments need one to cross provider borders, different packet technologies, traffic-engineered tunnels and access networks, where the two ends cannot always talk to each other directly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a multi-segment pseudowire as two or more contiguous segments that behave as a single point-to-point pseudowire, joined at a switching provider edge, and states the requirements for three setup mechanisms: static configuration, a pre-determined route, and a signalled dynamic route.
tldr.outcome: The document is a requirements statement, not a protocol. It covers architecture, resiliency, quality of service, congestion control, routing, operations and management, and separate security requirements for inter-provider and intra-provider cases.

today: RFC 5254 is an Informational document published in October 2008, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states requirements rather than defining a protocol, and it builds on the PWE3 architecture in RFC 3985 and the single-segment requirements in RFC 3916.

sections.title: Scope and Use Cases
sections.content:
The document specifies requirements for extending pseudowires across more than one packet-switched network domain, or across more than one packet network tunnel. These are called multi-segment pseudowires, and the requirements for single-segment pseudowires that extend edge to edge across only one domain are in RFC 3916. The document does not invalidate any part of the PWE3 architecture in RFC 3985, and the requirements it states apply only to multi-segment pseudowires, not to networks that support only single-segment ones.

Four situations make multi-segment pseudowires useful. Inter-provider pseudowires extend from a terminating edge in one provider's domain to one in another. A direct control channel between the two ends may not be possible, desirable or feasible: at a minimum, establishing one, such as a targeted LDP session, needs knowledge of and reachability to the far end's IP address, which the local end may not have because of operational or security constraints, and a single-segment pseudowire would also need a packet network tunnel between them, which may not be feasible or desirable for security or scalability reasons, or because the two domains use different technologies. Setup, maintenance and forwarding must also satisfy the constraints of a multi-provider environment; in the inter-AS layer 2 VPN scenario it is current practice to key all control traffic between two networks, and a multi-segment pseudowire lets the providers confine that key administration to the switching points that join the two domains.

PSN interworking is the second case: signalling protocols and packet network types may differ between provider networks, so a single-segment pseudowire is not possible, but a multi-segment pseudowire with the right interworking at the switching points can connect the ends.

Traffic-engineered tunnels and bandwidth-managed pseudowires are the third. Large provider networks need pseudowires deployed edge to edge, over hundreds or thousands of edge devices, with explicit bandwidth guarantees. A single-segment design would need a full mesh of traffic-engineered tunnels between all the provider edges, and inter-provider pseudowires riding such tunnels add to the count. What is needed is a sparse mesh of tunnels and signalling adjacencies, or a partition of the network into smaller pseudowire domains, and either way a pseudowire has to pass through more than one tunnel hop.

Pseudowires in access and metro networks are the fourth. Service providers want pseudowire technology in access and metro networks to cut maintenance complexity and cost, but today such networks are legacy TDM, SONET/SDH or Frame Relay/ATM, Ethernet, or IP based, and circuits are handled as attachment circuits in their native format at the edge of the IP-MPLS network, which means several separate access networks and complicates end-to-end control, provisioning and maintenance. With multi-segment pseudowires, access and metro elements need only maintain signalling adjacencies with the provider edges they connect to, rather than with every other access device, and a pseudowire from one access element to another can run in three segments: access element to provider edge, provider edge to provider edge, and provider edge to access element.
sections.plainLanguage: Four situations call for a wire that is stitched from several pieces: joining two operators' networks, joining networks that use different technologies, carrying traffic over reserved bandwidth without a full mesh of tunnels, and reaching into access networks that use older equipment.

sections.title: The Architecture and Its Vocabulary
sections.content:
The reference models are derived from the PWE3 architecture. In the basic configuration, a packet network tunnel extends between two edges of a single domain, carrying a pseudowire whose endpoints are those edges. The multi-segment model extends this: a terminating provider edge at each end provides the service to the customer equipment, the two ends terminate different packet network tunnels, which may sit in different packet network or pseudowire domains, and a switching provider edge in the middle joins a pseudowire in the first tunnel to a pseudowire in the second. The switching edge is the point where one segment becomes another, and it switches between segments based on the pseudowire identifiers, such as the PW label in the case of MPLS pseudowires. Segments of the same multi-segment pseudowire may be of the same pseudowire type or different types, and the tunnels may be the same or different technologies, though this document requires support only for segments of the same type.

Although the second figure shows a single switching edge, a pseudowire may pass through more than one. In the multi-AS case, a pseudowire from the edge of one autonomous system to the edge of another is composed of three segments: one inside the first autonomous system, one between the two border routers, which are the switching edges, and one inside the second autonomous system. The two autonomous systems may belong to the same provider, for instance an access network and a core network, or to two different providers.

The vocabulary follows PWE3, with four additions. A terminating provider edge is a provider edge where the customer-facing attachment circuits are bound to a pseudowire forwarder, and it appears at the first and last segments of a multi-segment pseudowire. A single-segment pseudowire is set up directly between two provider edge devices, with each direction traversing one packet network tunnel. A multi-segment pseudowire is a static or dynamically configured set of two or more contiguous pseudowire segments that behave and function as a single point-to-point pseudowire, and each of its ends must terminate on a terminating provider edge. A pseudowire segment is a single-segment pseudowire, or a part of a multi-segment one, set up between two provider edge devices. A switching provider edge is a provider edge capable of switching the control and data planes of the preceding and succeeding segments; it terminates the tunnels carrying them, and it is never both the switching point and the terminating edge for the same multi-segment pseudowire. A switching point runs the protocols needed to set up and manage segments with other switching points and terminating edges.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of box appear. The two ends terminate the customer's circuit, and the box in the middle stitches one segment of the virtual wire to the next. A single-segment pseudowire has no middle box; a multi-segment one has at least one.

sections.title: Three Ways to Set One Up
sections.content:
The requirements assume the use cases are realized with one or more of three mechanisms. Static configuration means the switching points, as well as the terminating edges, are manually provisioned for each segment. A pre-determined route means the pseudowire is established along an administratively determined route using an end-to-end signalling protocol, with automated stitching at the switching points. A signalled dynamic route means the pseudowire is established along a dynamically determined route using an end-to-end signalling protocol with automated stitching at the switching points, the route being selected with the help of one or more dynamic routing protocols.

The route of a pseudowire is defined here as the set of switching points the multi-segment pseudowire passes through between a given pair of terminating edges. The packet network tunnels along that route can be explicitly specified, or locally selected at the switching and terminating points, and the routing of the tunnels themselves is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to build the wire. You can configure every box by hand, you can tell the ends a fixed path through the network, or you can let the network work out the path and stitch it as it goes.

sections.title: The Requirements on the Mechanism
sections.content:
Several requirements apply to every mechanism. Where multi-segment pseudowires are tunnelled across a packet network that supports only single-segment ones, only the single-segment requirements apply to that network, and the fact that the overlay is carrying multi-segment pseudowires must be transparent to its routers. The pseudowires themselves must remain transparent to the P-routers, which are neither switching nor terminating edges and must have no knowledge of the pseudowires traversing them. Multi-segment pseudowires must use the same encapsulation modes as single-segment ones and must be composed of single-segment pseudowires. They must be able to cross packet networks of every technology PWE3 supports for single-segment pseudowires, with the switching edge providing the interworking when the technology changes. Both directions of a segment must terminate on the same switching or terminating edge, and switching edges may support only switching pseudowires of the same type, in which case the type is transparent in the forwarding plane.

On resiliency, mechanisms to protect a multi-segment pseudowire when an element on its path fails must be provided, and the generic requirements are that a backup pseudowire to a primary one should be supported along with a switchover on failure detection; that an end-to-end backup path should be configurable, whether statically, specified for signalling, or selected dynamically; that the primary and backup paths should be able to traverse separate switching points; that a primary and a backup with a different terminating edge should be configurable; that automatic fast switchover should be provided; and that automatic reversion to the primary may be provided, and must be configurable if it is.

On quality of service, pseudowires are intended to support emulated services such as TDM and ATM that may have strict per-connection requirements, including absolute or relative guarantees on loss, delay and jitter, delivered in part by reserving network resources and providing per-packet treatment. For single-segment pseudowires a traffic-engineered tunnel can ensure sufficient resources are reserved in the P-routers, and the terminating edges must be able to request those resources automatically, for admission control and accounting, with bandwidth management per class of service where the tunnel supports several. For multi-segment pseudowires, each switching edge maps a segment to a tunnel, and solutions must let the edges bind a segment to a tunnel automatically based on class of service and bandwidth when those are specified, and must be able to request tunnel resources per class of service. The edges must be able to associate a class-of-service marking with the pseudowire's packets, and must be able to translate markings at administrative domain boundaries, because different domains may use different values to mean the same treatment.

On congestion, the PWE3 architecture requires pseudowires to respond to path congestion by reducing their rate, and permits pseudowires without a congestion control mechanism to transmit over explicitly reserved capacity. Applied to multi-segment pseudowires, this means they must either employ a congestion control mechanism effective across the whole path, or have sufficient capacity reserved in every domain along the path before transmission starts, and switching edges are required to reject attempts to establish a segment for a pseudowire type that has no appropriate congestion control, or when sufficient resources cannot be reserved. Each domain must individually control congestion, and multi-segment pseudowires must not transmit across unprovisioned best-effort paths in the absence of another scheme. Solutions must let the edges on the path notify each other of congestion, indicated by queue length, loss rate or bandwidth measurement crossing a threshold, and the reaction may vary by pseudowire type, since some such as TDM pseudowires are more sensitive than others. An edge that knows a link or tunnel is congested must not set up a new multi-segment pseudowire that uses it.

On setup, the mechanisms must accommodate the provider's practices, especially for security, confidentiality of service provider information and traffic engineering. The ability to select switching points and tunnels statically must be provided, so that a pseudowire can be forced through particular points to enforce security and administrative policies, and solutions should minimise the amount of configuration needed and should support different setup mechanisms on the same equipment and network. The terminating edges must be able to support single-segment signalling as well as multi-segment signalling at the same time, and solutions must ensure a multi-segment pseudowire is set up when a path satisfying its bandwidth, class-of-service and other constraints exists. The setup procedures must be clearly defined so that a setup on the terminating edges can be read as successful only when all segments are up. Admission control against available resources must be performed at each segment and must be configurable, and if the tunnel lacks the resources, a new tunnel or a capacity increase may be attempted, with the pseudowire failing if that does not succeed. Finally, a segment must be settable up between two directly connected switching points with no tunnel at all, which lets a pseudowire cross autonomous system boundaries without a tunnel, with admission control on the link instead.

On routing, multi-segment pseudowires must be able to traverse multiple provider administrative domains, multiple autonomous systems within one administrative domain, multiple autonomous systems in different administrative domains, and any hybrid combination of these, including both transiting and terminating in a domain.
sections.plainLanguage: The mechanism has to keep working when a box in the middle fails, has to promise the customer the same quality of service across every domain it crosses, has to notice congestion and react, and has to be able to say yes only when there is really a path with enough bandwidth. It must also be able to cross from one operator's network to another's.

sections.title: Operations and Management
sections.content:
Operations and management are vital for pseudowires, and the mechanism must allow the management of a multi-segment pseudowire from the terminating edge to the other end, from the switching points and the other terminating edge. Single-ended monitoring should be supported for both directions. The single-segment mechanisms, such as the connectivity verification described in RFC 5085, should be extended to support multi-segment pseudowires on both an end-to-end and a segment basis, and all provider edge routers along the path must agree on a common mechanism to use. At the switching edge, defects on a packet network tunnel must be propagated to all the pseudowires that use that tunnel, and the directionality of defect notifications must be maintained across the edge. The switching edge should be able to behave as a segment endpoint for the monitoring mechanisms and must be able to pass end-to-end messages through transparently. Performance monitoring is required for both multi-segment and single-segment pseudowires, to measure round-trip delay, one-way delay, jitter and packet loss ratio.

On management, each approach that uses multi-segment pseudowires should provide mechanisms for operators to manage the emulated service, and those mechanisms must offer at least the capabilities defined for single-segment pseudowires. It should also be possible to manage the additional attributes of a multi-segment pseudowire. Since the operator that starts the setup may sit in a different packet network domain from the switching points and one of the terminating edges, mechanisms for remote management should be provided, and the management information base tables must be designed to help configure and provision the pseudowire at the switching and terminating edges and to support inter-domain configuration and monitoring of the attachment circuits. Remote management must be possible, and it should be possible to switch it off for security reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: The wire has to be checkable and fixable. The operator needs to see faults and measure delay, jitter and loss along the whole path and in each piece of it, and needs to be able to manage the setup from whichever end started it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document states requirements for multi-segment pseudowires set up across domain boundaries run by one or more providers, and for those set up within one provider. The security requirements for setup across domains administered by a single provider are those in the setup and requirement documents, and they also apply to the inter-provider case.

On the data plane, the concern is packets from within a multi-segment pseudowire travelling to a provider edge or attachment circuit the pseudowire is not meant to be connected to, and packets from outside entering it, in either case other than in a way consistent with the pseudowire's policy. Where a pseudowire crosses a provider border, there is a chance that packets could be falsely inserted at the originating, terminating or transit domains, by a malicious attack or a fault in the switching edge, and solutions may provide end-to-end authenticity for the packets. At a provider border, an edge should discard a packet received from a neighbour unless the label it processes was either distributed to that neighbour, or distributed to a peer beyond that neighbour, in which case the path is known to be via that neighbour. One of the domains crossed may decide to mirror the packets for eavesdropping, or to hijack them by directing them away from their destination, and in either case the privacy of the pseudowire is violated. The document places no requirement on protecting the privacy of the packets by encryption, though encryption may be required at a higher layer. The data plane of an edge at a domain boundary must be able to police incoming traffic to the pseudowire's traffic parameters or an administratively configured profile, and must be able to police or filter the monitoring messages. An ingress edge must ensure the pseudowire receives the class of service configured or signalled for it, and must guard against packets marked for a better class of service than they should receive, and must be able to define a separate label space per interface or per group of interfaces, so that it does not accept labelled packets from another provider unless the bottom label is one it assigned on the arriving interface.

On the control plane, the concern is that pseudowire connections are not accepted from anywhere, or a local attachment circuit could be connected to an arbitrary remote one, with the fault starting at a remote terminating edge or a switching edge. Where a segment crosses a provider border, the segment endpoints should be on the border routers between the two providers; interconnecting them over a physically secure link and enabling signalling and routing authentication eliminates the possibility of receiving a message or packet from an untrusted peer. The configuration and maintenance protocol must provide strong authentication and data protection for the control protocol, and a signature for each individual setup message must be available in addition to session-level authentication. Because switching edges in different provider networks should sit at the end of a physically secure link, or be joined by a limited number of trusted tunnels, each has a trust relationship with only a limited number of peers, so manual key management is expected to suffice, and a mechanism based on RFC 4107 must be developed if large-scale connections to other autonomous systems become necessary. Peer authentication protects against address spoofing but does not stop one peer connecting to the wrong attachment circuit, which under one authority is usually a misconfiguration and across providers may be deliberate, so static manual configuration gives a greater degree of security, and an incoming request or reply must not be accepted unless its source address is known to belong to an eligible peer, with peering restricted to eligible peers and to specific interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things must not happen: a packet from outside slipping into the wire, and a wire being connected to the wrong customer circuit. At a border between operators the boxes must check labels, police the traffic against what was agreed, and only accept setup messages from peers they already trust.

items.title: Inter-provider pseudowires
items.text: The two ends are in different operators' networks and may not be able to talk directly.

items.title: PSN interworking
items.text: The two halves use different signalling or packet network technologies.

items.title: Traffic-engineered tunnels
items.text: Bandwidth guarantees are needed, and a full mesh of tunnels does not scale.

items.title: Access and metro networks
items.text: Pseudowire technology is wanted closer to the customer, on older equipment.
